look_here_first: Both this species and Ludwigia repens have opposite leaves on creeping stems. Find an axillary flower: palustris has four green sepals and no yellow petals. Do not rely only on absent petals because repens may be apetalous or shed petals. Check the ovary/mature capsule: palustris typically has four longitudinal dark-green bands across its faces; repens does not.

morphology_keys.habit: Creeping/decumbent perennial of wet mud and shallow water; roots at nodes.
morphology_keys.leaves: Opposite, small elliptic to obovate, generally entire.
morphology_keys.flower: Minute axillary flowers with four usually green sepals; petals absent (not merely hidden). Usually four stamens.
morphology_keys.fruit: Short 2–5 mm 4-sided capsule with four green longitudinal bands, one across each face; compare with L. repens often longer 4–10 mm fruits that lack these characteristic bands. Fruit length overlaps and is supporting only.
best_field_traits: opposite leaves on creeping rooting stems shared with L. repens
petal-less tiny flower with four green sepals (repens sometimes loses/lacks petals too)
four dark-green longitudinal bands on ovary/capsule are the strongest confirmed separation from L. repens
short 2–5 mm capsule, though size overlaps repens
avoid guessing species from vegetative aquatic mats only

comparisons.key_distinctions: Palustris usually lacks petals and has four green capsule bands. L. repens may show tiny yellow petals, BUT may sometimes lack them as well: its mature capsule lacks palustris' four green longitudinal bands. Opposite foliage/creeping growth by themselves are shared and non-diagnostic.
